summary: Rodent efficacy findings did not reliably predict clinical efficacy: O'Collins et al. 2006 found similar mean neuroprotection in focal ischemia for drugs tested only in animals (24.4%) and drugs used clinically (31.3%, p>0.05), and translation rates ranged 0–100% (Ritskes‑Hoitinga et al. 2022). Many preclinical studies (82%) reported positive findings, suggesting publication/selection bias.
direction: evidence does not favour the model
why_range_is_wide: Translation rates came from heterogeneous studies and outcomes across reviews and were affected by publication bias and selective reporting.

direction: evidence does not favour the model

summary: Monticello et al. 2017: rodent toxicology showed modest sensitivity (48%) and PPV (43%) but higher specificity (84%) and NPV (86%), so rodent findings only partially tracked human adverse effects. summary: Dogs moderately predict human cardiac safety: Valentin et al. 2022 found 91% of drugs that prolonged QT in humans also prolonged QT in dogs (88% concordant negatives; 31% discordant), and Pollard et al. 2017 reported dog QTc AUC ≈0.81. Bhatt et al. 2019 gave combined BP/HR sensitivity 78% and specificity 79%, and Sadko et al. 2024 observed moxifloxacin +16.6 ms QTc in dogs (human ≈10 ms); concordance varies by endpoint and exposure.
why_range_is_wide: Variation arises by endpoint (QTc vs BP/HR), assay type and exposure level, and dataset composition (e.g. inclusion/exclusion of β2‑agonists).
negative_controls: Sadko et al. 2024: mock/vehicle produced no QTc increase (negative control).
